newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gaddum-Bonn should convert debt to Euros from 99.
newsitem.headline: Gaddum-Bonn should convert debt to Euros from 99.

text.p: Bundesbank Deputy President Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said on Wednesday that it was in Germany's interest to convert existing government debt into Euros from the start of the planned 1999 launch of the single currency.
Such a move would secure sufficient market liquidity for bonds and prevent a split in the market which would lead to a loss of liquidity and competitiveness, Gaddum said in a speech.
Germany has yet to decide when to transform its existing bonds into Euros.

Gaddum also said he was optimistic the government would one day be able to announce its bond issue plans for a full year, thereby meeting international standards. At present it announces issue calendars each quarter.

"Beyond the regular quarterly issue calendar there is really only the question when and perhaps if the government will issue (10-year or 30-year) bonds," Gaddum said in the text of a speech prepared for delivery at a stock market conference.
"But here too we are confident that refined fiscal planning will one day permit a complete annual calendar, which has become the international standard in recent years."

Gaddum also said preparation for the introduction of stripping -- separate trading of principal and interest for certain bonds -- was well under way and that he was confident it would be launched next year as announced.
"That will enable institutional investors in particular to cover the whole of the yield curve," Gaddum said.
Germany this year started issuing short-term government debt to boost market liquidity and help develop the bond market ahead of the Euro's launch when it will lose its main attraction, the mark.
The government also pledged to issue 30-year debt each year provided market conditions allowed it.

"If the federal government carries out its intention to serve the 30-year segment of the market once a year, we believe that as regards instruments and issue procedures we will be able to meet all challenges arising from the disappearance of the mark," Gaddum said.
